exult

/ɪɡˈzʌlt/ — ig-ZULT, stress on second syllable · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To exult is to show great joy and triumph in an open, jubilant way, especially after winning or succeeding at something.

The fans exulted in the streets after the championship victory.

Example

When the astronauts' spacecraft touched down safely on Mars, mission control erupted into celebration, and the lead engineer couldn't restrain herself—she leaped from her chair, arms raised, tears streaming down her face.

Exult captures not just happiness but the intense, uninhibited joy and triumph of a major achievement. 'Celebrate' or 'rejoice' alone wouldn't convey the sense of overwhelming triumph and the physical expression of it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

celebrate: To celebrate is to mark a success with festivity — a party, a cake, music — and it is something people plan and organize. To exult is what bursts out before any party is planned: leaping, cheering, openly reveling in a triumph. You can celebrate calmly; no one exults calmly.

rejoice: To rejoice is to feel and show great gladness, and the gladness can be entirely quiet — felt in stillness as easily as in song. To exult is louder and prouder: triumphant joy that bursts out in cheers and raised arms. Rejoicing can be hushed; exulting never is.

triumph: To triumph is to win and to glory openly in the victory — the word needs a rival or an obstacle that has just been defeated. To exult is to pour out the joy itself, and you can exult over plain good news with no opponent anywhere in sight.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

despair: to lose all hope completely

mourn: to grieve openly over a loss

Where it sits · how openly the delight bursts out — contentment → happiness → joy → exult

contentment vs. exult: Contentment is the quietest feeling on this scale: calm, settled satisfaction, a world away from the loud, leaping celebration of someone who exults.

happiness vs. exult: Happiness is stronger than contentment but weaker than exulting — happiness smiles, while to exult is to cheer, leap, and openly revel in a triumph.

joy vs. exult: Joy is intense gladness, yet exult goes one step further: joy is the feeling itself, while to exult is to let that joy burst out in visible, triumphant celebration.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out (Latin)

Root — ult

Root — ult: to leap (from Latin salire/sult-, 'to leap'; in exsultare the s of the root merged into the x)

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- ('out') + ult ('to leap,' from Latin salire — the s of the root merged into the x long ago): to exult is literally 'to leap out,' exactly the way joy makes winners jump into the air in triumph.

Use the root in a new word: somersault

Use the root in a new word: somersault: A somersault is literally a 'leap over' — the same Latin leaping root sal/sult that makes exult mean leaping out with joy after a victory.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / literary

Exult is a grand word for overwhelming joy and triumph — the feeling you can't contain. For everyday happiness, simpler words like 'happy' or 'pleased' fit better. Reach for exult when the joy is powerful and the occasion is significant.
